newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Qatar natural gas deal in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Qatar natural gas deal in doubt.

text.p: Israel has informed Enron Corp that it no longer has an exclusive agreement to negotiate with Qatar for natural gas supplies for Israel, a National Infrastructure Ministry spokesman said on Thursday.
"A letter to this effect was sent to Enron in late September informing the company of our decision," the spokesman said.

Enron and Israel signed a memorandum of understanding in October 1995 at an economic conference in Amman granting the Houston-based company 180 days to finalise an agreement with Qatar for the supply of at least two million tonnes a year of natural gas.

The agreement, signed by former Israeli energy minister Gonen Segev and Enron Development Corp chief executive Rebecca Mark, gave Enron exclusivity in negotiations with Qatar during this 180-day period.
The Israeli daily Haaretz reported on Thursday that Qatar has expressed anger over the Jewish state's decision.
However the Israeli spokesman said he was unaware of any official protest over the matter.

Qatar and Oman have forged ahead of other Gulf states in establishing economic ties with Israel but have stopped short of full diplomatic relations pending the resolution of all Arab-Israeli conflicts.

Qatar, meanwhile, has put further normalisation on hold, including postponing the opening of a trade office in Israel. This followed the recent outbreak of violence between Israelis and Palestinians that killed 75 people and cast doubts on the future of the Middle East peace process.

The Infrastructure Ministry spokesman said Israel decided not to renew the agreement with Enron since no deal was reached with Qatar during the 180-day period. However, he stressed, this did not mean that Enron could not continue to negotiate with Israel towards reaching a deal.

The Qatari gas was expected to be substantially more expensive than other sources of natural gas such as Egypt since the proposal called for shipping it the form of liquefied natural gas (LNG) on tankers and then for regasification at a plant estimated to cost $300 million.

Shortly after taking office Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon decided that Israel would negotiate with various potential suppliers of natural gas and would not depend on a sole supplier for national security reasons.
Talks are under way with Egypt, Russia and other potential suppliers.
